entries.title: Trouble whichever way one turns
entries.odia:
ଏଣୁ ମାଇଲେ ଗୋ ହତ୍ୟା
ତେଣୁ ମାଇଲେ ବ୍ରହ୍ମ ହତ୍ୟା।
entries.literal_meaning: Strike this way, and it is cow-killing; strike that way, and it is the killing of a Brahmin.
entries.meaning_odia: ଏପଟେ ଗଲେ ଏକ ଅନର୍ଥ, ସେପଟେ ଗଲେ ଆଉ ଏକ ଅନର୍ଥ—କୌଣସି ପଥ ସହଜ ବା ନିରାପଦ ଲାଗୁନଥିବା ଦୋସନ୍ଧିର କଥା। କେଉଁ କାମଟି କରିବା ଉଚିତ, ତାହା ନିର୍ଣ୍ଣୟ କରିବା କଠିନ ହୁଏ।
entries.explanation: Either direction seems to lead to a serious wrong. The Odia Vasa gloss explains this as a dilemma in which one cannot decide what to do. The two religiously charged acts give force to the feeling that no available choice is harmless.
entries.usage_example: Two urgent responsibilities require the same limited time; attending to either means failing the other. Someone might use the saying to express that bind. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The saying frames both cow-killing and Brahmin-killing as grave wrongs within its religious vocabulary. The balanced this way / that way construction closes off an easy escape and turns that imagery into an expression of indecision.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line182, ଏଣୁ ମାଇଲେ ଗୋ ହତ୍ୟା.

entries.title: Experience becomes knowledge
entries.odia: ଏ ସନ ମଳୁ, ଆର ସନକୁ ବଇଦ।
entries.literal_meaning: A patient this year; a healer by next year.
entries.meaning_odia: ନିଜେ କୌଣସି ଅବସ୍ଥା ଭୋଗିଲେ ସେ ବିଷୟରେ ଅଭିଜ୍ଞତା ହୁଏ। ଏ ବର୍ଷର ରୋଗୀ ଆର ବର୍ଷକୁ ବଇଦ ହେବାର ଚିତ୍ରରେ ଅନୁଭବରୁ ଜ୍ଞାନ ମିଳିବାର କଥା କୁହାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: Going through something can teach a person how it works. The verse compresses that learning into a reversal of roles: the patient becomes the healer. The inspected Odia Vasa gloss reads it as gaining knowledge through experience.
entries.usage_example: After working through a difficult application process, someone can explain its steps to the next applicant. The saying could acknowledge knowledge acquired firsthand. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The contrast between this year and next year gives the change a compact time frame. ମଳୁ names the ill person and ବଇଦ the healer: the verse moves from receiving help to having knowledge that can help someone else.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line186, ଏ ସନ ମଳୁ, ଆର ସନକୁ ବଇଦ.

entries.title: A fitting place and welcome words
entries.odia:
ଏମିତି ସଜରେ ବସି ଯାଇଥିବ
କେହି ନ କହିବେ ଉଠ୍
ଏମିତି ମଜାରେ କହି ଯାଉଥିବ
କେହି ନକହିବେ ଝୁଟ୍।
entries.literal_meaning: Sit in such a manner that no one says, “Get up.” Speak so pleasantly that no one says, “False.”
entries.meaning_odia: ଅନ୍ୟଙ୍କ ସହ ମିଶିବା ବେଳେ ବସିବାର ଢଙ୍ଗ ଓ କଥା କହିବାର ଭଙ୍ଗୀ ପ୍ରତି ଧ୍ୟାନ ଦେବାର ଉପଦେଶ। ନିଜ ଉପସ୍ଥିତି ଯେପରି ଅଶୋଭନ ନହୁଏ ଓ ନିଜ କଥା ଯେପରି ଅବିଶ୍ୱାସ ନଜନ୍ମାଏ, ସେପରି ଆଚରଣ କରିବାକୁ କୁହାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The two pairs of lines ask the listener to avoid a rebuff: being told to leave a seat, or having a statement dismissed as false. Read as advice, they connect considerate conduct with speech that others can receive with confidence. The force lies in attending to how one’s presence and words affect others.
entries.usage_example: Before joining a group discussion, a newcomer is advised to take a suitable place and speak thoughtfully, without exaggeration. The verse could frame that advice. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The short replies ଉଠ୍ and ଝୁଟ୍ give the advice its rhyme and its sharpness. One interrupts a person’s sitting; the other interrupts their speech. The balanced lines imagine conduct that gives no occasion for either rebuff.

entries.title: Bold words, sudden retreat
entries.odia:
ଏସା କରେଙ୍ଗା
ତେସା କରେଙ୍ଗା
ସିପାହୀ ଦେଖିଲେ ଶୋଇ ପଡ଼େଙ୍ଗା।
entries.literal_meaning: “I will do this, I will do that”—but at the sight of a soldier, I will lie down.
entries.meaning_odia: କଥାରେ ବହୁତ ସାହସ ଦେଖାଇବା, କିନ୍ତୁ ଅସଲ ପରୀକ୍ଷା ଆସିଲେ ଡରି ପଛେଇଯିବାକୁ ଏହି ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କହେ। ପ୍ରଥମ ଦୁଇ ପଦର ବାହାଦୁରି ଶେଷ ପଦରେ ଭାଙ୍ଗିଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: The speaker announces one bold action after another, then becomes timid as soon as a soldier appears. The inspected Odia Vasa gloss identifies the target as someone who claims fearlessness in words but loses courage when action is required. The ending punctures the earlier boast.
entries.usage_example: Someone loudly promises to challenge an unfair decision, but falls silent when the person responsible arrives. The saying could tease that gap between promise and action. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Hindi-influenced କରେଙ୍ଗା and ପଡ଼େଙ୍ଗା rhyme around the Odia phrase ଦେଖିଲେ ଶୋଇ. The repeated boasts build momentum, and the last line abruptly turns confident speech into a picture of retreat.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line196, ଏସା କରେଙ୍ଗା.

entries.title: Finding faults in a cumin seed
entries.odia:
ଋଷି ଘରକୁ ମହାଋଷି ଗଲେ
ଜିରା ଭିତରୁ ଶିରା କାଢିଲେ।
entries.literal_meaning: A great sage went to a sage’s house and drew a vein out of cumin.
entries.meaning_odia: ଜିରା ଭଳି ଛୋଟ ଜିନିଷରୁ ଶିରା କାଢ଼ିବା ଚିତ୍ରରେ ଅଯଥା ଦୋଷ ଖୋଜିବାକୁ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କରାଯାଇଛି। ଋଷିଙ୍କ ଘରକୁ ମହାଋଷି ଆସିବାର କଥା ଏହି ଖୁଣ ଧରିବାକୁ ଆହୁରି ନାଟକୀୟ କରେ।
entries.explanation: The tiny cumin seed becomes the object of an extravagant search for faults. An inspected idiom gloss explains drawing a vein from cumin as needless fault-finding. Read through that idiom, the visiting great sage turns supposed distinction into an occasion for petty criticism.
entries.usage_example: A reviewer ignores the substance of a sound proposal and keeps raising trivial objections. Someone could use the couplet to question that fault-finding. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The progression from sage to great sage raises expectations of wisdom. The second line reduces the visitor’s achievement to extracting something minute from cumin. That contrast supplies the editorial reading of exaggerated discernment becoming pettiness.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line198, ଋଷି ଘରକୁ ମହାଋଷି ଗଲେ.

entries.title: A covered face, a carrying voice
entries.odia:
ଓଢଣା ପଡିଛି ନାକ ସରିକି
ତୁଣ୍ଡ ଶୁଭୁଅଛି ଚଉପାଢ଼ୀକି।
entries.literal_meaning: The veil reaches the nose, yet the voice can be heard as far as the meeting pavilion.
entries.meaning_odia: ନାକ ଯାଏ ଓଢଣା ଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ କଥାର ସ୍ୱର ଚଉପାଢ଼ୀ ଯାଏ ଶୁଭୁଛି—ଏହି ବିପରୀତ ଚିତ୍ରରେ ବାହାରର ସଂଯତ ରୂପ ଓ ଉଚ୍ଚ ସ୍ୱରର କଥା ମଧ୍ୟରେ ଅମେଳକୁ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କରାଯାଇଛି। ଏହା କଥକଙ୍କ ଟିପ୍ପଣୀ; ନାରୀ ଚୁପ୍ ରହିବା ଉଚିତ ବୋଲି ଉପଦେଶ ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The saying contrasts a face covered to the nose with a voice carrying far beyond it. Its teasing force depends on the speaker treating the covered appearance as reserved, while hearing something much more conspicuous. Our reading identifies that contrast without making quietness a duty for women.
entries.usage_example: In an imagined reading discussion, someone points out how the covered face and far-carrying voice pull in opposite directions. The group can discuss the speaker’s expectations as well as the image itself. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ଚଉପାଢ଼ୀ names a meeting pavilion or village school in the inspected dictionary. Here it gives the voice a destination beyond the covered face. A modern fictional use places the saying in a grandmother’s rebuke, showing a gendered judgement in that particular scene.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line200, ଓଢଣା ପଡ଼ିଛି ନାକ ସରିକି.

entries.english_summary: The speaker contrasts a covered face with a voice that carries far.

entries.title: What shapes the result
entries.odia:
ଓଳି ଗୁଣେ କୋଳି
ପଲମ ଗୁଣେ ସରୁ ଚକୁଳି।
entries.literal_meaning: The berries take their quality from the soil; the thin chakuli takes its quality from the pan.
entries.meaning_odia: ମାଟି ଗୁଣେ କୋଳି ଓ ପଲମ ଗୁଣେ ଚକୁଳି ହେବାର ଉପମାରେ ଯେଉଁ ପରିବେଶରେ କିଛି ଗଢ଼େ, ତାହାର ପ୍ରଭାବକୁ କୁହାଯାଇଛି। ଦେଖାଯାଇଥିବା ସଂକଳନର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଏହାକୁ ପିଲାଙ୍କ ଉପରେ ପିତାମାତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଭାବ ସହ ଯୋଡ଼େ।
entries.explanation: The couplet pairs the ground in which berries grow with the pan on which chakuli is made. Both images connect a result to what helps shape it. The inspected compilation applies that comparison to parents and children; here it is read as an image of formative influence, not a fixed judgement of a child from their family.
entries.usage_example: A discussion about children’s habits turns to the examples adults set at home. The saying could introduce the influence of that environment. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ପଲମ is an earthen pan and ଚକୁଳି a flat cake; ସରୁ draws attention to thinness. The two compact comparisons bring cultivation and cooking together before the source gloss applies them to family influence.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line202, ଓଳି ଗୁଣେ କୋଳି.
witnesses.note: Supports first-word repair from upload ଓଳ to ଓଳି. Remaining wording agrees; uploaded line break retained. Shared lineage possible.

witnesses.locator: ଓ-section item15, inspected public page line692.

entries.title: Troublesome company joins forces
entries.odia:
ଓଲୁଅ ତିଆରେ ବଣ ସାରୁକୁ
ତୋର ମୋର ଯିବା ବିଭାଘରକୁ।
entries.literal_meaning: Olua, the arum, urges the wild taro: “You and I will go to the wedding.”
entries.meaning_odia: ଓଲୁଅ ଓ ବଣସାରୁ ଏକାଠି ବିଭାଘରକୁ ଯିବାର ଚିତ୍ର ଦୁଇ ଅନିଷ୍ଟକାରୀ ଲୋକଙ୍କ ମେଳକୁ ବୁଝାଏ। ଦେଖାଯାଇଥିବା ସଂକଳନର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଅନୁସାରେ, ସେମାନେ ଏକାଠି ହେଲେ ଭଲ କାମରେ ବିଘ୍ନ ଘଟିପାରେ।
entries.explanation: Two plants are given voices and set off together for a wedding. The inspected Odia Vasa gloss applies the pairing to two troublesome people whose combined presence disrupts a good undertaking. The emphasis is on their joining forces, not merely resembling one another.
entries.usage_example: Two people who repeatedly derail meetings decide to attend the same planning session together. Someone might use the saying to express concern about their combined disruption. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The wedding supplies the scene of a shared occasion, while the plants become a pair of would-be guests. The compact exchange makes an alliance visible before the source gloss turns it into a warning about company that causes trouble.

entries.title: Small thefts become a habit
entries.odia:
କଖାରୁ ଚୋର, ଲାଉ ଚୋର
ଚୋରାଉ ଚୋରାଉ ବଡ଼ା ଚୋର।
entries.literal_meaning: A pumpkin thief, a bottle-gourd thief—stealing and stealing, a big thief.
entries.meaning_odia: ଛୋଟ ଛୋଟ ଚୋରିକୁ ବାରମ୍ବାର କରୁଥିଲେ ସେହି ଅଭ୍ୟାସ ବଡ଼ ଅନ୍ୟାୟ ଆଡ଼କୁ ନେଇଯାଇପାରେ। କଖାରୁ ଓ ଲାଉ ଚୋରିରୁ ବଡ଼ ଚୋର ହେବାର ଚିତ୍ରରେ ଏହି ସତର୍କତା ରହିଛି।
entries.explanation: The saying follows a pattern from stealing ordinary vegetables to becoming a bigger thief. Its repeated stealing and stealing makes the growth of a habit audible. The inspected source gloss supports this warning about repeated small thefts developing into more serious wrongdoing.
entries.usage_example: Someone keeps taking small amounts from a shared fund and dismisses each incident as insignificant. The saying could warn against allowing that conduct to become routine. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Pumpkin and bottle gourd give the warning concrete objects before the final phrase enlarges the scale. The repeated word for thief links the beginning and ending, while the repeated verb supplies the steps between them.

entries.title: Either way, the count stays five
entries.odia:
କର୍ଣ୍ଣ ମଲେ ପାଞ୍ଚ
ଅର୍ଜୁନ ମଲେ ପାଞ୍ଚ।
entries.literal_meaning: If Karna dies, five; if Arjuna dies, five.
entries.meaning_odia: ଯେଉଁ ପଟର ଘଟଣା ଘଟୁନା କାହିଁକି, ଶେଷରେ ସଂଖ୍ୟା ବା ସ୍ଥିତି ସମାନ ରହିବାର କଥା। କର୍ଣ୍ଣ ଓ ଅର୍ଜୁନଙ୍କ ନାମ ବଦଳିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଦୁଇ ପଦର ଶେଷରେ ପାଞ୍ଚ ହିଁ ରହୁଛି।
entries.explanation: Two different outcomes leave the same total. The inspected compilation explains the proverb as a situation in which number or position remains unchanged. Its repeated five places the emphasis on that unchanged result, even though the two named people differ.
entries.usage_example: A team fills one vacant place by moving someone from another team, leaving the same total number of vacancies. Someone could use the saying to point out that the overall position has not improved. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The source connects the lines with Karna and Kunti in the Mahabharata: in its account, either Karna or Arjuna would survive and Kunti would still have five sons. That numerical contrast explains the refrain without requiring a retelling of the surrounding epic.

entries.title: Talk grows, thread wears thin
entries.odia:
କଥାକୁ ମାଜିଲେ ମୋଟା
ସୂତାକୁ ମାଜିଲେ ସରୁ।
entries.literal_meaning: Rub a matter over and it grows thicker; rub a thread and it grows thinner.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗୋଟିଏ କଥାକୁ ଧରି ବାରମ୍ବାର ଆଲୋଚନା କରି ଚାଲିଲେ ତାହା କ୍ରମେ ବଡ଼ ହୋଇଯାଏ। ସୂତାକୁ ମାଜିଲେ ସରୁ ହୁଏ, କିନ୍ତୁ କଥାକୁ ସେହିପରି ଘାଣ୍ଟିଲେ ତାହା ଆହୁରି ବଢ଼େ।
entries.explanation: Repeatedly going over a matter can make it grow in importance and extent. The proverb contrasts that growth with a thread becoming thinner through rubbing. The inspected source gloss focuses on dwelling on a matter again and again until it becomes larger.
entries.usage_example: A small disagreement is brought up at every meeting until it overshadows the work itself. Someone could use the saying to point out how repeated discussion has enlarged the quarrel. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The same verb, ମାଜିଲେ, joins two opposite results: a matter becomes thick or large, while a thread becomes thin. That compact reversal turns a familiar physical action into an image of how words can magnify an issue.

witnesses.locator: Inspected public page line219, କଥାକୁ ମାଜିଲେ entry.

entries.title: Every fruit tastes astringent
entries.odia:
କରମ ଦଶା
ଯେ ଫଳ ଖାଇଲେ ସେ ଫଳ କଷା।
entries.literal_meaning: Such is my lot: whichever fruit I eat is astringent.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦୁର୍ଭାଗ୍ୟ ଏମିତି ଲାଗି ରହିଛି ଯେ ଯାହା ବାଛିଲେ ବି ମନମୁତାବକ ଫଳ ମିଳୁନାହିଁ—ଏହି ହତାଶାର କଥା। ଯେଉଁ ଫଳ ଖାଇଲେ ବି କଷା ଲାଗିବାର ଚିତ୍ରରେ ବାରମ୍ବାର ନିରାଶ ହେବାର ଅନୁଭବ ପ୍ରକାଶ ପାଏ।
entries.explanation: The speaker describes a run of disappointment as bad luck: even choosing a different fruit brings the same unwelcome taste. This editorial reading treats the line as an expression of frustration when nothing seems to turn out well.
entries.usage_example: After several carefully chosen plans fall through, someone sighs that every choice seems to bring another disappointment and recalls this saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Fruit offers the prospect of an enjoyable taste, but every fruit here turns out astringent. The repeated ଯେ ଫଳ … ସେ ଫଳ makes disappointment seem to follow every choice, while କରମ ଦଶା names the speaker’s sense of an unfortunate lot.

entries.title: Who can rewrite fate?
entries.odia:
କରମ ଲିଖନ
କେ କରିବ ଆନ ?
entries.literal_meaning: Who can alter what fate has written?
entries.meaning_odia: ଭାଗ୍ୟରେ ଯାହା ଲେଖା ଅଛି, ତାହାକୁ କିଏ ବଦଳାଇ ପାରିବ—ଏହି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନରେ ଘଟଣାକୁ ନିଜ ନିୟନ୍ତ୍ରଣ ବାହାରର ବୋଲି ମାନିନେବାର ସ୍ୱର ଅଛି। ଭାଗ୍ୟକୁ ଏଠାରେ ବଦଳାଇ ହେଉନଥିବା ଲେଖା ପରି କଳ୍ପନା କରାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The question voices resignation: what has happened feels already written and beyond the speaker’s power to change. Its image is of destiny as a written record whose words cannot be altered. This is an editorial reading of the saying’s literal rhetorical question.
entries.usage_example: After an unexpected cancellation ends a long-awaited visit, someone accepts the disappointment with “Who can rewrite fate?” This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ଲିଖନ turns destiny into writing, while ଆନ asks whether that writing can be made different. The unanswered question carries the sense that the speaker sees no way to change the outcome.

entries.title: If you act, why fear?
entries.odia:
କରୁ ଯଦି ଡ଼ରୁ କାହିଁକି
ଡରୁ ଯଦି କରୁ କାହିଁକି ?
entries.literal_meaning: If you do it, why are you afraid? If you are afraid, why do you do it?
entries.meaning_odia: କୌଣସି କାମ କରିବାକୁ ନିଷ୍ପତ୍ତି ନେଇ ପୁଣି ଡରରେ ଦୋଦୁଲ୍ୟମାନ ହେବାକୁ ଏହି କଥା ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କରେ। କରିବାକୁ ଯାଉଛ ଯଦି ଡରୁଛ କାହିଁକି, ଆଉ ଡରୁଛ ଯଦି ସେ କାମରେ ପଶୁଛ କାହିଁକି—ଦୁଇ ପଟରୁ ସେହି ଦ୍ୱିଧାକୁ ଧରିଛି।
entries.explanation: The two questions challenge the tension between choosing an action and shrinking from it. Reversing do and fear makes the listener confront that hesitation from both directions. This editorial reading takes it as a pointed challenge to indecision.
entries.usage_example: Someone volunteers to present a rehearsed poem, then repeatedly backs away from taking the stage. A friend might use these questions to challenge the hesitation. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The second line turns the first around: doing comes before fearing, then fearing before doing. The repeated କାହିଁକି gives both halves the same questioning pressure and makes the saying easy to remember.

entries.title: Have the backing before you begin
entries.odia:
କଳି ଯେବେ କରିବସିବ
ସଙ୍ଗେ ଥିବ ଭାଇ
ଦୁଧ ଯେବେ ଖାଇ ବସିବ
ଘରେ ଥିବ ଗାଈ।
entries.literal_meaning: When you enter a quarrel, have a brother beside you; when you sit down to drink milk, have a cow at home.
entries.meaning_odia: କୌଣସି କାମରେ ପଶିବା ପୂର୍ବରୁ ତାହା ପାଇଁ ଦରକାରୀ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ଓ ସାଧନ ଥିବା କଥା। କଳି ବେଳେ ପାଖରେ ଭାଇର ସାହାରା ଓ ଦୁଧ ପାଇଁ ଘରେ ଗାଈ—ଏହି ଦୁଇ ଚିତ୍ରରେ ଆଶା ସହିତ ତାହାର ଆଧାରକୁ ଯୋଡ଼ାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: Each half pairs an intention with something that supports it: a brother’s presence in a quarrel, a cow as a source of milk. Read more broadly, the saying asks whether the necessary backing or means are in place before an undertaking begins. This broader reading is editorial.
entries.usage_example: A group promises a large community meal before arranging ingredients and helpers. Someone recalls the saying to bring the discussion back to the people and supplies needed. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The rhyme ଭାଇ / ଗାଈ links human support with a household resource. One stands beside the speaker; the other supplies what the speaker wants. Their parallel positions give the two scenes a shared practical point.

entries.title: A smooth talker can sell rotten shrimp
entries.odia:
କହି ପୋଛି ପାରେ ଯେ
ପଚା ଚିଙ୍ଗୁଡି ବିକେ ସେ।
entries.literal_meaning: Whoever can talk persuasively can sell rotten shrimp.
entries.meaning_odia: ଚତୁର ଭାବରେ କଥା କହି ଅନ୍ୟକୁ ମନାଇ ପାରୁଥିବା ଲୋକ ଖରାପ ଜିନିଷକୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ବିକି ପାରେ। ପଚା ଚିଙ୍ଗୁଡିର ଚିତ୍ରରେ କଥାର ଚମକ ଓ ଜିନିଷର ଅସଲ ମାନ ମଧ୍ୟର ଫରକ ଧରାପଡ଼େ।
entries.explanation: Persuasive speech can make even an undesirable thing seem worth buying. The rotten shrimp give the saying its sharp edge: selling skill and the quality of what is sold are two different things. The inspected article uses a close variant to illustrate the power of salesmanship.
entries.usage_example: An enthusiastic sales pitch makes a badly worn item sound like an exceptional bargain. A listener recalls the saying while looking past the pitch to inspect the item. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The image places polished speech beside spoiled goods. That contrast allows the line to acknowledge verbal skill while making the listener aware of what the words may conceal.

witnesses.locator: Opening discussion of online sales; paragraph beginning ବିକ୍ରୀ କରି ଜାଣିଲେ, indexed excerpt inspected17November2026.
witnesses.note: Variant କହି-ବୋଲି ପାରିଲା ଯିଏ, ପଚା ଚିଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ି ବିକି ପାରିଲା ସିଏ. Confirms rotten-shrimp sales image and persuasive-talk reading, not exact uploaded ପୋଛି wording. Direct page open failed; indexed article excerpt includes byline/date and this context. Public ଚିଙ୍ଗୁଡ଼ି differs orthographically from uploaded display ଚିଙ୍ଗୁଡି, which is retained.

entries.english_summary: A convincing pitch can hide the poor quality of what is offered.
entries.narrative_credit: Translation and interpretation by Project Odisha, informed by the sources below.

entries.title: Words can cook a lavish feast
entries.odia:
କହିବାର କଥା, କି’ ଯାଉଚି
ନଅଟା ଧାନରେ ଛଅଟା ଚକୁଳି
ଦି’ ପାଖେ ଘିଅ ବୋହି ଯାଉଛି।
entries.literal_meaning: It is only talk—what does it cost? From nine grains of paddy, six chakuli pancakes, with ghee flowing down both sides.
entries.meaning_odia: କହିବାକୁ କିଛି ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚ ନାହିଁ ବୋଲି ଲୋକ ଅସମ୍ଭବ କଥା ବି ବଢ଼ାଇ କହିପାରେ। ନଅଟି ଧାନରୁ ଛଅଟି ଚକୁଳି, ପୁଣି ଦୁଇ ପାଖରୁ ଘିଅ ବହୁଛି—ଏହି ଅତିଶୟୋକ୍ତିରେ ଫମ୍ପା ବଡ଼ କଥାକୁ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କରାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The opening makes talk costless; the next lines demonstrate how extravagantly someone can speak. Nine grains supposedly produce six pancakes, then even those are described as overflowing with ghee. The widening gap between scant ingredients and lavish results makes this an editorially clear image of empty boasting.
entries.usage_example: Someone promises an elaborate event with almost no funds and no practical arrangements. A listener uses the saying to question the abundance promised by words alone. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The humour builds in stages: a tiny count of grains becomes several pancakes, then ghee flows from both sides. The kitchen image gives exaggerated claims a concrete scale that a listener can picture.

entries.english_summary: Costless talk promises absurd abundance from almost nothing.

entries.title: Alike in colour, different in voice
entries.odia:
କାଉ କୋଇଲି ଏକା ବର୍ଣ୍ଣ
ରାବିଲା ବେଳେ ଭିନ୍ନ ଭିନ୍ନ।
entries.literal_meaning: The crow and koel are the same colour; when they call, they sound different.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦେଖିବାକୁ ଏକା ପରି ଲାଗିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ କଥାବାର୍ତ୍ତା ବା ପ୍ରକାଶରେ ଫରକ ଜଣାପଡ଼େ। କାଉ ଓ କୋଇଲିର ରଙ୍ଗର ସାମ୍ୟ ସହ ସେମାନଙ୍କ ଅଲଗା ରାବକୁ ମିଳାଇ ଏହି କଥା କୁହାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: Outward resemblance does not tell the whole story. In the saying, birds that look alike are distinguished as soon as they call. Applied to people, the image suggests that speech or expression can reveal differences that appearance leaves hidden; this application is editorial.
entries.usage_example: Two presenters arrive in equally polished clothes, but their explanations reveal very different levels of preparation. A listener recalls the saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The verse moves from seeing to hearing. Its first half groups the two birds together by colour; the repeated ଭିନ୍ନ in the second separates them through their voices. That change of sense carries the comparison.

witnesses.locator: Page9, two lines beginning କାଉ କୋଇଲି ଏକା ବର୍ଣ୍ଣ.
witnesses.note: Rendered upload inspected17November2026; readable wording and line break retained.

entries.english_summary: Similar appearances can conceal differences revealed by voice.

entries.title: A leaf and salt, but claims of three dishes
entries.odia:
କାଖରେ ପତର, ହାତରେ ଲୁଣ
ମିଛରେ ବୋଲଇ ତିନି ତିଅଣ।
entries.literal_meaning: A leaf under the arm, salt in the hand—yet falsely claiming three dishes.
entries.meaning_odia: ହାତରେ ଯାହା ଅଛି ତାହା ସାମାନ୍ୟ, କିନ୍ତୁ କହିବା ବେଳେ ବହୁତ କିଛି ଅଛି ବୋଲି ମିଛ ଦାବି କରିବା। ପତର ଓ ଲୁଣ ସହ ତିନି ତିଅଣର କଥାକୁ ମିଳାଇ ବାସ୍ତବ ସମ୍ବଳ ଓ ବଡ଼ କଥାର ଫରକ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The first line lists what can actually be seen: a leaf and salt. The second announces a much richer meal and explicitly calls that announcement false. The editorial reading is of someone overstating what they have or can offer.
entries.usage_example: Someone advertises a fully equipped workshop, though only a few basic tools are available. A visitor recalls the saying to contrast the claim with the actual provision. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The leaf and salt make a sparse food image; three cooked dishes suggest something more substantial. The word ମିଛରେ makes the criticism explicit, so the contrast turns on false boasting rather than on having little.

witnesses.locator: Page9, final two-line saying beginning କାଖରେ ପତର.
witnesses.note: Rendered upload inspected17November2026; clear wording retained. Interpretation editorial; no independent attestation claimed.

entries.english_summary: A meagre provision is dressed up as a generous offering.
entries.narrative_credit: Translation and interpretation by Project Odisha, informed by the sources below.

entries.title: The wood’s own brother helps cut it
entries.odia:
କାଠ କହିଲା- ମୋତେ କିଏ ହାଣୁଚି ?
ତୋ’ ଭାଇ ତା ଭିତରେ ପଶି ହାଣୁଚି।
entries.literal_meaning: The wood asked, “Who is cutting me?” “Your brother has entered it and is cutting you.”
entries.meaning_odia: ନିଜ ପକ୍ଷର ଜଣେ ବିରୋଧୀଙ୍କ ସହ ମିଶି ନିଜ ଲୋକଙ୍କ କ୍ଷତି କରାଇବାର କଥା। କୁରାଢ଼ିରେ ଲାଗିଥିବା କାଠ ବେଣ୍ଟକୁ କାଠର ଭାଇ ବୋଲି ଦେଖିଲେ ଉପମାଟି ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ ହୁଏ—ନିଜ ଜାତିର ଜିନିଷ ହିଁ ଆଘାତର ସାଧନକୁ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ କରୁଛି।
entries.explanation: The inspected public variant makes the axe the respondent and explains the saying as harm enabled by someone from one’s own side. The wooden handle supplies the natural reading of the wood’s brother: something akin to the victim has become part of the instrument that hurts it.
entries.usage_example: A member secretly gives a rival group the information needed to undermine a shared project. The others use the saying to describe the help the rival received from within. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The little dialogue personifies wood and turns shared material into kinship. Calling the handle a brother makes the injury more pointed: the cutting depends on wood’s own kind. The longer public form names the axe, while the upload leaves that part implicit.

witnesses.locator: Page10, two-line dialogue beginning କାଠ କହିଲା.
witnesses.note: Rendered page inspected17November2026. Concise wording retained, with unnamed respondent and ତା ଭିତରେ.

entries.odia_summary: ନିଜ ପକ୍ଷର ଲୋକ ବିରୋଧୀଙ୍କୁ ସାହାଯ୍ୟ କରି ନିଜ ଲୋକଙ୍କ କ୍ଷତି କରାଇବା।
entries.english_summary: Harm from outside is enabled by someone from within.
entries.narrative_credit: Translation and interpretation by Project Odisha, informed by the sources below.

entries.title: Ears without gold, gold without ears
entries.odia:
କାନ ଥିଲେ ସୁନା ନାଇଁ
ସୁନା ଥିଲେ କାନ ନାଇଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: When there are ears, there is no gold; when there is gold, there are no ears.
entries.meaning_odia: ଇଚ୍ଛା ଥିବାବେଳେ ସମ୍ବଳ ନାହିଁ, ଆଉ ସମ୍ବଳ ଥିବାବେଳେ ଇଚ୍ଛା ନାହିଁ—ଦୁଇଟି ଏକାଠି ନମିଳିବାର କଥା। କାନ ଓ ସୁନାର ଏହି ଓଲଟା ଯୋଡ଼ାରେ ଦରକାରୀ ଦୁଇ ପଟରୁ ଗୋଟିଏ ସବୁବେଳେ ଅଭାବ ରହୁଛି।
entries.explanation: Two things that would serve each other fail to arrive together. The inspected source explains the contrast as having the desire without the money, then the money without the desire. The repeated reversal gives that mismatch a rueful, memorable form.
entries.usage_example: Someone long wanted to learn an expensive hobby but could not afford it; years later, the money is available and the interest has faded. They recall this saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The pairing evokes gold worn at the ear. Each line supplies one half and withdraws the other, so the value of having either is frustrated by the absence of its counterpart.

witnesses.locator: Page10, two-line saying beginning କାନ ଥିଲେ.
witnesses.note: Rendered page inspected17November2026; uploaded ନାଇଁ retained twice.

witnesses.locator: କ-section item140, line952, inspected17November2026.
witnesses.note: Variant has ନାହିଁ twice. Explicit gloss compares wealth without desire and desire without wealth.

variants.odia:
ଦାନ୍ତ ବେଳକୁ ଚଣା ନାଇଁ
ଚଣା ବେଳକୁ ଦାନ୍ତ ନାଇଁ।
variants.locator: Uploaded compilation page24, third item.
variants.note: Related alternate expression grouped editorially with the ears/gold reversal; replaces adornment/desire with eating/physical capacity. No established textual descent. Literal: When there are teeth, there are no chickpeas; when there are chickpeas, there are no teeth. ଅର୍ଥ: ଦାନ୍ତ ଥିବାବେଳେ ଚଣା ମିଳୁନାହିଁ, ଆଉ ଚଣା ମିଳିବାବେଳେ ଦାନ୍ତ ନାହିଁ। ଯାହାକୁ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରିବାକୁ ଚାହୁଁଛୁ ଓ ତାହା କରିବାର ସାମର୍ଥ୍ୟ ଏକ ସମୟରେ ନମିଳିବାର ଆକ୍ଷେପ ଏଥିରେ ପଢ଼ାଯାଇଛି। Explanation: The two lines exchange what is present and absent. Food and the means of chewing it fail to coincide. This is a concrete counterpart to the ears/gold reversal: it changes adornment and desire to eating and physical capacity. No particular person’s ageing or financial history is stated. Source: uploaded compilation page24, inspected17November2026; exact ନାଇଁ retained. Source quotation excluded from collection CC licensing; no licence for upload established.

entries.english_summary: The desire and the means fail to coincide.

entries.title: Making fuel cakes when the rains arrive
entries.odia:
କାଳକ ଯାକ ଥିଲା ବସି
ଆଷାଢ଼ ମାସରେ ପାରୁଛି ଘସି।
entries.literal_meaning: Idle all that time, now laying out dung cakes in Ashadha.
entries.meaning_odia: ସୁବିଧାର ସମୟରେ କାମ ନକରି ବସି ରହିବା, ଆଉ ଅନୁକୂଳ ସମୟ ଗଲା ପରେ କାମ ଆରମ୍ଭ କରିବା। ଶୁଖିବା ଦରକାର ଥିବା ଘସିକୁ ବର୍ଷା ମାସରେ ପାରିବାର ଚିତ୍ରରେ କାମ ପକାଇ ରଖିବାର ଅସୁବିଧା ଧରାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The source gloss identifies a person who keeps putting work off. The image makes the cost of delay concrete: fuel cakes need to dry, but their preparation has been postponed until the rains. Beginning at last does not recover the favourable conditions already lost.
entries.usage_example: Someone leaves an outdoor repair untouched through dry weather and starts only when repeated rain makes the job difficult. A neighbour recalls the saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ଘସି are dried dung cakes used as fuel. Setting their preparation against Ashadha gives the verse its seasonal irony: the task depends on drying, yet the long-idle worker begins in a rainy period.

witnesses.locator: Page10, two lines beginning କାଳକ ଯାକ ଥିଲା ବସି.

entries.title: Long in darkness, now two torches
entries.odia:
କାଳକ ଗଲା ଅନ୍ଧାର ଘର
ଲାଗିଚି ଏବେ ଯୋଡି ମଶାଲ।
entries.literal_meaning: So much time passed with the house dark; now a pair of torches is lit.
entries.meaning_odia: ଦୀର୍ଘ ସମୟ ଧରି ଅଭାବ ଥିବା ଜାଗାରେ ଏବେ ବେଶି ଆୟୋଜନ ହୋଇଥିବାର ବିପରୀତ ଚିତ୍ର। ଆଗର ଅନ୍ଧାର ଘର ଓ ଏବର ଯୋଡ଼ି ମଶାଲକୁ ଏକାଠି ରଖି ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନଟିକୁ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The saying places a long period without light beside the arrival of two torches. Its explicit contrast is between earlier lack and present abundance. This edition reads it as a pointed observation on how conspicuously circumstances have changed.
entries.usage_example: A meeting room goes without basic equipment for years, then receives an elaborate new setup. Someone recalls the contrast between the dark house and its two torches. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The house stays the same while its illumination changes. A pair of torches makes the new provision stand out against the earlier darkness, and ଏବେ marks the turn from then to now.

entries.title: Familiarity understands the gesture
entries.odia: କାଲ ଠାର କାଲ ମା ଜାଣେ।
entries.literal_meaning: A mother understands the gestures of her deaf child.
entries.meaning_odia: ଯାହା ସହିତ ନିତି ଚଳପ୍ରଚଳ ଓ ଘନିଷ୍ଠତା ଥାଏ, ତାଙ୍କର ଇଙ୍ଗିତ, ଉଦ୍ଦେଶ୍ୟ ଓ ସ୍ୱଭାବ ଭଲ ଭାବରେ ବୁଝିହୁଏ। ମାଆ ନିଜ ଶ୍ରବଣହୀନ ସନ୍ତାନର ଠାର ବୁଝିବାର ଚିତ୍ରରେ ସେହି ପରିଚୟର ଶକ୍ତି ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: Close and repeated contact makes another person’s meaning easier to understand. The inspected source gloss emphasizes knowing someone’s intentions and ways through everyday association. The mother and child provide the saying’s concrete image of that familiarity.
entries.usage_example: Two longtime colleagues understand a small gesture during a busy performance, while a newcomer needs the cue explained. Someone recalls the saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The focus is a familiar gesture and the person who recognizes it. The mother-child relationship makes the repeated attention behind that recognition easy to picture.

variants.odia: ଭୀମ ବଳ କୁଇନ୍ତାକୁ ଜଣା।
variants.locator: Page32, first item beginning ଭୀମ ବଳ.
variants.note: Related-family wording grouped editorially with POD-DHAGA-406 for close maternal knowledge; no textual descent asserted. Literal reading: Bhima’s strength is known to Kuinta. Odia meaning: ଭୀମଙ୍କ ବଳ କୁଇନ୍ତାଙ୍କୁ ଜଣା—ଏହା ପଙ୍କ୍ତିର ସିଧା କଥା। ଆମ ସମ୍ପାଦକୀୟ ପାଠରେ, ଘନିଷ୍ଠ ପରିଚୟ ଥିବା ଲୋକ ଜଣଙ୍କ ପ୍ରକୃତ ସାମର୍ଥ୍ୟ ଜାଣିଥାନ୍ତି। କୁଇନ୍ତା ନାମର ମୂଳ ବନାନ ରଖାଯାଇଛି; ଯାଞ୍ଚ କରାଯାଇଥିବା ସାର୍ବଜନୀନ ପ୍ରତିରୂପରେ ଏହା ଭୀମଙ୍କ ମାଆ କୁନ୍ତୀଙ୍କ ନାମରେ ବ୍ୟବହୃତ। Interpretive reading: The saying places knowledge of Bhima’s strength with Kuinta, identified as his mother Kunti in the inspected public counterpart. Read editorially, a close acquaintance can know a person’s real capacity. The wording neither says that only she knows nor supplies a particular episode proving the strength. Name reference: Satya Prakash, କଥାଣି୨, section21, https://satyaprakashsethy.com/କଥାଣି-୨/ , inspected17November2026, identifies କୁଇନ୍ତା as mother Kunti; its wording differs. Uploaded spelling retained without repair. No epic-origin claim. Source quotation has unknown rights and is excluded from the collection’s original editorial-content licence.

entries.title: An ascetic since yesterday, already with matted locks
entries.odia: କାଲିକା ଯୋଗୀ -ମୁଣ୍ଡରେ ଜଟା।
entries.literal_meaning: Yesterday’s ascetic—matted locks already on the head.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅଳ୍ପଦିନର ଅନୁଭବ ଥାଇ ମଧ୍ୟ ବହୁଦିନର ଅଭିଜ୍ଞ ଲୋକ ପରି ବଡ଼ କଥା କହିବା ବା ଚିହ୍ନ ଦେଖାଇବା। ନୂଆ ଯୋଗୀଙ୍କ ମୁଣ୍ଡରେ ଜଟାର ଚିତ୍ର ଦେଇ ଅଭିଜ୍ଞତା ପୂର୍ବରୁ ତାହାର ଆଡ଼ମ୍ବରକୁ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କରାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The source applies the saying to an inexperienced person making grand claims. The joke lies in the timing: someone has only just taken on a role, yet already displays a sign associated in the image with long practice. The appearance has arrived ahead of the experience.
entries.usage_example: After one introductory class, someone begins presenting themselves as a seasoned expert. A friend recalls the saying to question the inflated claim. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The public gloss treats matted locks on a newly become ascetic as a suspect shortcut to an established appearance. The verse uses that compressed contrast to make premature authority visible.

entries.title: Yesterday’s situation is different today
entries.odia: କାଲିକା କଥା ଆଜିକୁ ଅନ୍ତର।
entries.literal_meaning: Yesterday’s state of affairs is different by today.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗତକାଲି ଯେପରି ଅବସ୍ଥା ଥିଲା, ଆଜି ସେପରି ରହିନାହିଁ। ସଂସାର ଓ ପରିସ୍ଥିତି ବଦଳୁଥାଏ—କାଲି ଓ ଆଜିର ଛୋଟ ବ୍ୟବଧାନରେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଫରକ ଆସିପାରେ।
entries.explanation: The saying observes that circumstances change, even across the short distance between yesterday and today. The inspected source gloss gives this general sense of a changing world. It invites a fresh look at the present situation.
entries.usage_example: A plan made yesterday needs revising after the available arrangements change overnight. Someone recalls the saying while checking what is possible now. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: There is no elaborate story: yesterday and today stand side by side. Their closeness makes the change feel immediate, while ଅନ୍ତର supplies the contrast.

entries.title: Sweets for some, harsh greens for others
entries.odia:
କାହା କରମରେ ଖିରି ଖିରିସା
କାହା କରମରେ ଲଡୁ
କାହା କରମରେ ଖାରିଆ ଖଡା
ଚୋବାଇ ଚୋବାଇ ମରୁ।
entries.literal_meaning: Some are allotted khiri and khirisa puddings, some laddus; others harsh-tasting greens—chew and chew until you die.
entries.meaning_odia: କାହା ଭାଗରେ ସୁଆଦିଆ ମିଠା ଖାଦ୍ୟ, ଆଉ କାହା ଭାଗରେ କଷ୍ଟରେ ଚୋବାଇ ଖାଇବା ଶାଗ—ଏହି ତୁଳନାରେ ଲୋକଙ୍କ ଭିନ୍ନ ଭିନ୍ନ ଅବସ୍ଥାକୁ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି। କରମର କଥା କହି ଏହି ଅସମାନ ଭାଗ୍ୟ ଉପରେ ଖେଦ ପ୍ରକାଶ ପାଏ।
entries.explanation: The repeated opening distributes very different meals to different people. Puddings and sweets stand against greens presented as an exhausting mouthful. This editorial reading hears a complaint about unequal comfort and hardship, expressed through the language of fortune.
entries.usage_example: People compare how some have every comfort while others struggle for ordinary necessities. Someone recalls the contrast between sweets and endlessly chewed greens. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The first two lines name sweet foods; the third changes the taste and texture, and the repeated chewing slows the last line down. That movement makes unequal portions feel like unequal experiences of life.

entries.title: A measure of grain for one, straw for another
entries.odia:
କାହା ମୁହଁକୁ ଧାନ ଭରଣେ
କାହା ମୁହଁକୁ ପାଳ ଭରଣେ।
entries.literal_meaning: To one person’s mouth, a measure of paddy; to another’s, a measure of straw.
entries.meaning_odia: କାହାକୁ ଉପକାରୀ ଜିନିଷ ମିଳୁଛି, ଆଉ କାହାକୁ ସେହି ପରିମାଣରେ ଅନୁପଯୋଗୀ ଜିନିଷ। ଧାନ ଓ ପାଳର ତୁଳନାରେ ଏକା ମାପର ଭାଗ ଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ତାହାର ମୂଲ୍ୟ ଓ ଉପକାର ସମାନ ନହେବାର କଥା ଦେଖାଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: Both portions are described by the same measure, but one contains grain and the other straw. The repeated quantity makes the unequal substance more striking. This edition reads the image as a contrast in what different people actually receive.
entries.usage_example: Two groups receive packages of the same size, but one contains useful supplies and the other mostly packing material. Someone recalls the saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Grain and straw come from the same crop but have different uses. Placing them before mouths sharpens the contrast between what can provide nourishment after preparation and what cannot serve that purpose for people.

entries.title: Prosperity for some, ruin for others
entries.odia:
କାହାର ପୁଷ ମାସ
କାହାର ସର୍ବନାଶ।
entries.literal_meaning: For some, the month of Pusha; for others, utter ruin.
entries.meaning_odia: ଏକ ସମୟରେ କାହାର ସୁଖ ଓ ସମୃଦ୍ଧି, ଆଉ କାହାର ବଡ଼ ବିପତ୍ତି। ପୁଷ ମାସର ଧନଧାନ୍ୟର ଭାବ ସହ ସର୍ବନାଶକୁ ରଖି ଲୋକଙ୍କ ଅବସ୍ଥାର ତାରତମ୍ୟ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: Different people can experience the same period in radically different ways. Pusha stands for a fortunate, plentiful time, while the other half names total ruin. The inspected source gloss emphasizes this disparity in circumstances.
entries.usage_example: A sudden change in demand brings one business a busy season while another loses its customers. Someone uses the saying to describe the opposite outcomes. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The month name carries an association with grain and prosperity. Its rhyme with ସର୍ବନାଶ places abundance beside devastation, compressing a large difference in experience into two short lines.

entries.title: A few words that reach the heart
entries.odia:
କିଛି କହେ ନାହିଁ ସରମରେ
ପଦିଏ ପଦିଏ କହି ଦେଉଥାଏ
ବାଜି ଯାଉଥାଏ ମରମରେ।
entries.literal_meaning: Says nothing out of shyness; yet says a little phrase at a time, and it strikes deep in the heart.
entries.meaning_odia: ଲାଜରେ କିଛି କହେ ନାହିଁ ବୋଲି କୁହାଯାଉଛି, ଅଥଚ ପଦିଏ ପଦିଏ କଥା କହିଦିଏ ଯାହା ହୃଦୟକୁ ଛୁଇଁଯାଏ। ଅଳ୍ପ କଥା ମଧ୍ୟ ମନରେ ଗଭୀର ପ୍ରଭାବ ପକାଇପାରେ।
entries.explanation: The opening presents someone as too shy to speak, then immediately describes the few words they do say. Those short phrases reach deep into the listener’s feelings. This editorial reading preserves the contrast between apparent reticence and the force of a little speech.
entries.usage_example: A quiet friend says only a few words about a shared memory, but they stay with the listener long afterwards. The saying could describe that moment. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ସରମରେ and ମରମରେ link shyness with the inner heart through rhyme. The repetition ପଦିଏ ପଦିଏ slows the speech into small phrases, making their deep effect stand out.

entries.title: King by another’s strength
entries.odia: କୀଚକ ବାହୁବଳେ ବିରାଟ ରଜା।
entries.literal_meaning: By Kichaka’s strength of arm, Virata is king.
entries.meaning_odia: ନିଜ ସାମର୍ଥ୍ୟ ଅପେକ୍ଷା ଅନ୍ୟର ବଳ ବା ସାହସରେ କାହାର ଅଧିକାର ଓ ପ୍ରତିପତ୍ତି ରହିବା। କୀଚକର ବଳରେ ବିରାଟଙ୍କ ରାଜତ୍ୱର ଛବି ଦେଇ ଅନ୍ୟର ସାମର୍ଥ୍ୟ ଉପରେ ନିର୍ଭରତାକୁ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The title belongs to one person, while the strength sustaining it comes from another. The inspected proverb gloss applies the saying critically to someone whose position or advantages depend on another person’s courage or power.
entries.usage_example: A nominal leader claims all the credit, though a capable colleague handles every difficult negotiation. Someone recalls this saying about the strength behind the title. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The saying draws on Kichaka and King Virata from the Mahabharata. The inspected source gloss casts Kichaka as the source of the force supporting Virata’s rule, turning the two names into a compact image of dependent authority.

entries.title: Fed by one side, praising the other
entries.odia:
କୁରୁବଳଙ୍କର ଖାଉଛି
ପାଣ୍ଡବଙ୍କର ଗାଉଛି।
entries.literal_meaning: Eats from the Kuru side; sings of the Pandavas.
entries.meaning_odia: ଖାଇବା ବା ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ଗୋଟିଏ ପକ୍ଷଠାରୁ ମିଳୁଛି, କିନ୍ତୁ ଗୁଣଗାନ ହେଉଛି ଅନ୍ୟ ପକ୍ଷର। ଯେଉଁଠୁ ସମର୍ଥନ ମିଳେ ଓ ଯାହା ପାଇଁ ପ୍ରଶଂସା କରାଯାଏ, ସେ ଦୁଇଟିର ଅମେଳକୁ ଏହି କଥା ଦେଖାଏ।
entries.explanation: Food comes from one side, while the song goes to the other. Read as praise, the singing creates a pointed contrast between the source of someone’s support and the side they publicly favour. The inspected parallel makes a similar contrast using fighting for the other side.
entries.usage_example: One group supplies everything needed for an event, but the organiser publicly credits its rival. A member of the supporting group uses the saying to point out the mismatch. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The Kuru side and the Pandavas supply the opposing names from the Mahabharata. Eating and singing compress material support and public praise into a short contrast, without naming the person whose loyalties are being questioned.

entries.title: A son blamed for a family’s decline
entries.odia:
କୁଳ କ୍ଷୟ ବେଳକୁ
ଘୋଡ଼ାମୁହାଁ ପୁଅ ଜନ୍ମ।
entries.literal_meaning: When the family is nearing ruin, a horse-faced son is born.
entries.meaning_odia: ପରିବାରର ଅବନତି ସହ ଜଣେ ପୁଅକୁ ଅଯୋଗ୍ୟ ବୋଲି ଦୋଷ ଦେବାର କଠୋର କଥା। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟାରେ ଏହା ଅଯୋଗ୍ୟ ପୁତ୍ରକୁ ବୁଝାଏ; ଘୋଡ଼ାମୁହାଁ ହେଉଛି ଉକ୍ତିର ଅପମାନଜନକ ଛବି, ଚେହେରା ଦେଖି ଯୋଗ୍ୟତା ବିଚାର କରିବାର ଆଧାର ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The saying places the birth of a disparaged son beside the family’s decline. The inspected source gloss identifies the target as an unfit son. Its harsh image expresses blame and pessimism about the family’s future; physical appearance does not establish a person’s character or ability.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional family dispute, an elder quotes the saying while blaming an adult son’s reckless decisions for losses. The quotation reveals the elder’s harsh judgement. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The image joins continuity through a son with anxiety about the family line ending. The animal comparison intensifies the insult, while the timing makes the birth sound like a sign of impending ruin. These are features of the saying’s rhetoric.

entries.title: The fibre shares the flowers’ honour
entries.odia: କୁସୁମ ପରଶେ ପଟ ନିସ୍ତରେ।
entries.literal_meaning: Through the flowers’ touch, the banana fibre is delivered.
entries.meaning_odia: ଫୁଲ ସହ ରହି କଦଳୀପଟୁକା ମଧ୍ୟ ଆଦରର ସ୍ଥାନ ପାଏ। ସେହିପରି ଭଲ ଲୋକଙ୍କ ସଙ୍ଗ ଜଣକୁ ଉନ୍ନତି ଓ ସମ୍ମାନର ସୁଯୋଗ ଦେଇପାରେ।
entries.explanation: The fibre gains a place of honour because it is joined to flowers. The inspected gloss uses this image for the benefit someone receives through good company or a valued association. Here “delivered” carries the figurative sense of being raised to a better position.
entries.usage_example: A beginner joins a thoughtful group of craftspeople, learns from them and gains opportunities through their shared work. Someone recalls the saying about the value of good company. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ପଟ here is the banana-plant fibre used with flowers, rather than finished cloth. In the flower-and-fibre image, something ordinarily overlooked shares the flowers’ honoured place because the two are joined.

entries.title: A trayful lost, a handful hoped for
entries.odia:
କୁଲାକ ଚାଉଳ କୁକୁରକୁ ଦେଇ
ଖୁଦ ମୁଠାକୁ ତୋ ଆଶା?
entries.literal_meaning: After giving a winnowing-trayful of rice to a dog, you hope for a handful of broken rice?
entries.meaning_odia: ବହୁତ ସମ୍ପଦ ହାତରୁ ଯାଉଥିବାକୁ ଅବହେଳା କରି ସାମାନ୍ୟ ଲାଭକୁ ଆଶା କରିବା। କୁଲାଏ ଚାଉଳ ଛାଡ଼ି ଖୁଦ ମୁଠାଏ ଲୋଡ଼ିବାର ତୁଳନାରେ ଏହି ଅସଙ୍ଗତିକୁ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The question contrasts a large quantity already given away with a small amount still eagerly sought. The inspected gloss applies it to overlooking a substantial loss while concentrating on a minor gain. The focus is the mismatch in priorities.
entries.usage_example: Someone ignores a large unpaid debt but spends hours chasing a tiny refund. A friend recalls the saying to question where their attention is going. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: A winnowing tray and a handful make the difference in quantity visible. Whole rice is then contrasted with broken grains, so the hoped-for return looks smaller in both amount and quality. The final question sharpens the rebuke.

witnesses.locator: Page11 final line and page12 first line, beginning anomalous ଲୁଲାକ ଚାଉଳ.

entries.title: The grievance is remembered
entries.odia:
କୁଲାରେ କାଟିଲି ଲାଉ
ସବୁ ଦିନ କଥା ମନରେ ଅଛି
ଦିନେ ତ ସାଧିବି ଦାଉ।
entries.literal_meaning: I cut a bottle gourd on a winnowing tray; I remember the matters of all those days; one day I shall settle the score.
entries.meaning_odia: ଆଗର ସବୁ କଥା ମନେ ରଖି ଦିନେ ତାହାର ପ୍ରତିଶୋଧ ନେବାକୁ ବକ୍ତା କହୁଛି। ତୁରନ୍ତ କିଛି ନକଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଅସନ୍ତୋଷ ମନରୁ ଯାଇନାହିଁ; ଶେଷ ପଦରେ ପରେ ଦାଉ ସାଧିବାର ଧମକ ଅଛି।
entries.explanation: The speaker has kept earlier grievances in mind and promises to settle them later. The last line makes the intent sharper than merely remembering or postponing a reply. It voices a lingering grudge.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional quarrel, someone recalls several earlier slights and quotes the saying to make clear that the dispute is still alive. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The everyday image of cutting a bottle gourd on a winnowing tray opens the verse. ଲାଉ rhymes with ଦାଉ, carrying that ordinary image into the pointed promise at the end. The words supply no account of what originally caused the quarrel.

entries.title: What wedding calls for all this?
entries.odia: କେଉଁ ବାହାଘରକୁ ଦୁଇ ଗୋଡ଼ରେ ଅଳତା।
entries.literal_meaning: For what wedding is there alta on both feet?
entries.meaning_odia: ଅତି ସାମାନ୍ୟ କାମ ବା ଅବସର ପାଇଁ ବହୁତ ବଡ଼ ଆୟୋଜନ କରିବାକୁ ଏହି ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ଥଟ୍ଟା କରେ। ଦୁଇ ଗୋଡ଼ରେ ଅଳତା ଲଗାଇ ଏତେ ସଜ ହେବାକୁ କେଉଁ ବାହାଘର ଅଛି ବୋଲି ପଚାରି ଅବସର ଓ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତିର ଅମେଳ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The question mocks preparations that seem too elaborate for the occasion. The inspected gloss explicitly applies it to making a large arrangement for a minor event. The wedding adornment supplies the image of a level of preparation that the actual occasion scarcely calls for.
entries.usage_example: A brief informal visit is being planned like a grand reception. Someone uses the saying to question the scale of the arrangements. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Alta is a red cosmetic dye used to colour the feet. The saying itself pairs this adornment with a wedding, then questions whether there is an occasion substantial enough to warrant it.

entries.title: The ladle does not taste the curry
entries.odia:
କେତେ ଘାଣ୍ଟିବ ଘାଣ୍ଟୁ
ତିଅଣ ସୁଆଦ କି ଜାଣିବ ଚଟୁ?
entries.literal_meaning: Let it stir however much it will—can the ladle know the curry’s taste?
entries.meaning_odia: ଚଟୁ ତିଅଣକୁ ଯେତେ ଘାଣ୍ଟିଲେ ବି ତାହାର ସୁଆଦ ଜାଣିପାରେ ନାହିଁ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ, କେବଳ ପାଖରେ ରହିବା ବା ଏକ କାମକୁ ବାରମ୍ବାର କରିବାରୁ ତାହାର ମର୍ମ ବୁଝିହେବ ବୋଲି ନିଶ୍ଚିତ ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The ladle remains in contact with the food and keeps moving through it, yet cannot experience its flavour. This edition reads the image as a distinction between repeated involvement and understanding: going through the motions does not itself bring insight.
entries.usage_example: A learner repeats a passage flawlessly but has not considered what it means. A teacher recalls the ladle and curry to encourage attention to meaning. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The kitchen utensil does the stirring while taste belongs to someone who can experience the dish. Repetition of the stirring verb sets up the final question, which exposes the difference between contact and comprehension.

witnesses.locator: କ-section item230, line1109, inspected17November2026.

entries.title: Sometimes the cart carries the boat
entries.odia:
କେତେ ବେଳେ ସଗଡ଼ ଉପରେ ନାଆ
କେତେ ବେଳେ ନାଆ ଉପରେ ସଗଡ଼
entries.literal_meaning: Sometimes the boat is on the cart; sometimes the cart is on the boat.
entries.meaning_odia: ସମୟ ସହ ଅବସ୍ଥା ଓ ଭାଗ୍ୟ ବଦଳେ। କେବେ ଶଗଡ଼ ନାଆକୁ ବୋହେ, କେବେ ନାଆ ଶଗଡ଼କୁ ବୋହେ—ଏହି ଓଲଟା ସମ୍ପର୍କରେ ପରିସ୍ଥିତିର ପରିବର୍ତ୍ତନ ଦେଖାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The same two objects exchange positions: what carries at one time is carried at another. The inspected gloss reads this as changing fortune and reversed circumstances. A present advantage or dependence need not remain fixed.
entries.usage_example: A neighbour who once helped a family through a difficult period later needs that family’s help. Someone recalls the cart and boat as their roles change. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Both cart and boat are means of carrying things, yet each becomes the other’s load in turn. Reversing their order in the second line makes the change in circumstances visible and easy to remember.

entries.title: A waxed parting in grey hair
entries.odia:
କେମନ୍ତ କଥା
ପାକଲା ବାଳରେ ମହଣ ସୁନ୍ଥା।
entries.literal_meaning: What is this—a waxed parting in grey hair!
entries.meaning_odia: ପାଚିଲା ବାଳକୁ ମହଣ ଦେଇ ସୁନ୍ଥା କରି ସଜାଇବା ଦେଖି ବକ୍ତା ଆଶ୍ଚର୍ଯ୍ୟ ବା ଥଟ୍ଟା ପ୍ରକାଶ କରୁଛି। ଏହା ବକ୍ତାର ଦୃଷ୍ଟିଭଙ୍ଗୀ; ବୟସ ବଢ଼ିଲେ ସଜ ହେବା ଅନୁଚିତ ବୋଲି ନିୟମ ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The exclamation places grey hair beside a carefully waxed parting. This edition hears surprise or teasing in that contrast: the styling appears unexpected to the speaker. The line reveals that expectation rather than establishing how someone of a particular age ought to look.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional conversation, someone teases an older relative who has carefully styled their hair for a photograph by quoting these lines. The remark exposes the speaker’s expectations about age. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ମହଣ here means beeswax, whose use on combed hair is recorded in the inspected dictionary. ସୁନ୍ଥା is the hair parting. Together they give the image a precise grooming detail rather than a quantity or weight.

entries.title: Anger as enemy, understanding as friend
entries.odia:
କ୍ରୋଧ ଠାରୁ ଶତୃ ନାହିଁ
ବୋଧ ଠାରୁ ମିତ୍ର ନାହିଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: No enemy is greater than anger; no friend is greater than understanding.
entries.meaning_odia: କ୍ରୋଧକୁ ବଡ଼ ଶତ୍ରୁ ଓ ବୁଝିବାର ଶକ୍ତିକୁ ବଡ଼ ମିତ୍ର ବୋଲି ଏହି କଥା ତୁଳନା କରେ। ରାଗରେ ଚାଳିତ ହେବା ବଦଳରେ କଥାକୁ ବୁଝି ବିଚାର କରିବାର ମୂଲ୍ୟ ଏଥିରେ ଅଛି।
entries.explanation: The two lines give inner states the roles of enemy and friend. In this editorial reading, anger can work against a person’s interests, while understanding helps them respond with judgement. The force comes from the balanced contrast.
entries.usage_example: Before replying to an upsetting message, someone pauses to understand what happened and recalls the saying. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: କ୍ରୋଧ and ବୋଧ rhyme, while ଶତୃ and ମିତ୍ର form the opposing pair. The verse turns anger and understanding into imagined companions whose effects differ.

entries.title: A boon by anger or austerity
entries.odia: କୋପେ ବର ନଇଲେ ତପେ ବର।
entries.literal_meaning: A boon through anger; otherwise, a boon through austerity.
entries.meaning_odia: କୋପ ପ୍ରକାଶ କରି ହେଉ ବା ତପସ୍ୟା କରି ହେଉ, ଲକ୍ଷ୍ୟ ହେଉଛି ବର ପାଇବା। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଦେବତାଙ୍କଠାରୁ ବର ଲାଭର କଥା କହେ; ଉକ୍ତିଟି ଏକ ଫଳ ପାଇଁ ଦୁଇ ଭିନ୍ନ ପଥକୁ ପାଖାପାଖି ରଖିଛି।
entries.explanation: The desired boon stays the same while the means change. The inspected gloss places the contrast in seeking a boon from deities, either through a display of anger or through austerity. More broadly, the wording can suggest trying contrasting approaches to secure the same result.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional discussion, someone first presses an angry demand, then offers to undertake a difficult task to obtain the same concession. A listener recalls the saying about two routes to one boon. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: ବର means a granted boon in the inspected source’s religious frame. କୋପ and ତପ are paired by sound, setting anger beside ascetic effort while repeating the desired reward.

entries.title: Go a kos, gain a handful
entries.odia: କୋଶେ ଗଲେ ପୋଷେ ମିଳେ।
entries.literal_meaning: Go a kos, and a cupped handful is gained.
entries.meaning_odia: ଜୀବିକା ପାଇଁ ଘରୁ ବାହାରି ଦୂରକୁ ଗଲେ ନୂଆ ରୋଜଗାରର ସୁଯୋଗ ମିଳିପାରେ। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ନିଜ ଗାଁ ବାହାରେ କାମ କରି ଅଧିକ ଆୟ କରିବାର ଆଶା ସହ ଏହି କଥାକୁ ଯୋଡ଼େ।
entries.explanation: The short rhyme joins distance travelled with something gained. The inspected source applies it to earning a better livelihood away from one’s home village. It expresses the hope that venturing farther can open opportunities.
entries.usage_example: A craftsperson finds buyers at a market beyond their village and recalls the saying about going farther to earn. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: କୋଶ names a traditional distance measure; ପୋଷ is the amount held in a cupped palm. Their rhyme compresses a journey and its hoped-for return into a few words, without naming a precise wage or quantity of goods.

entries.title: The servant became the mistress
entries.odia:
ଖଡ଼ୁ ବିକି କରି ରଖିଲଇ ଦାସୀ
ସେ ହେଲା ସାଆନ୍ତାଣୀ
ମୁଁ ପରବାସୀ।
entries.literal_meaning: I sold bangles and kept a female servant; she became the mistress of the household, and I a stranger living away from home.
entries.meaning_odia: ଖଡ଼ୁ ବିକି ଯାହାକୁ ଦାସୀ ଭାବେ ରଖାଗଲା, ସେ ସାଆନ୍ତାଣୀ ହେଲା; ଯିଏ ରଖିଥିଲା, ସେ ପରବାସୀ ହେଲା। ନିଜ ସମ୍ବଳ ଦେଇ ଆଣିଥିବା ସାହାଯ୍ୟ ଶେଷରେ ନିଜ ସ୍ଥାନ ହରାଇବା ସହ ଯୋଡ଼ିଯିବାର ଅଭିଯୋଗ ଭାବେ ଏହାକୁ ପଢ଼ାଯାଇଛି।
entries.explanation: The speaker begins by paying a personal cost to retain help. By the end, the person brought in as a servant occupies the position of mistress, while the speaker is away from home. This editorial reading hears a complaint about a reversal of power that leaves its original provider displaced.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional tale, a character gives up valuables to bring someone into the household, then loses their own place there. A reader compares that reversal with these lines. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The bangles make the initial sacrifice concrete. ଦାସୀ, ସାଆନ୍ତାଣୀ and ପରବାସୀ then trace the change in position through three roles: servant, household mistress and displaced speaker. The verse leaves the means of that reversal untold.

entries.title: Which virtue of the date palm shall I praise?
entries.odia:
ଖଜୁରୀ ଗଛର କି ଗୁଣ ଗାଇବି
ସେତ ମୂଳରୁ ପାହାଚ ପାହାଚ।
entries.literal_meaning: What virtue of the date palm shall I sing? From its very base, it is step after step.
entries.meaning_odia: ଯାହାର ସବୁଆଡ଼େ ଦୋଷ ଭରି ରହିଛି, ସେଥିରୁ ଗୋଟିଏ ଦୋଷ ବାଛି କହିବାର ଅର୍ଥ ନାହିଁ—ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଏହିପରି। ଗୁଣ ଗାଇବାର ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ଏଠାରେ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ; ମୂଳରୁ ପାହାଚ ପାହାଚର ଛବିରେ ଦୋଷର ପୁନରାବୃତ୍ତି ଦିଶେ।
entries.explanation: The opening offers praise in form, but the inspected gloss makes it ironic. When faults run throughout something, selecting just one is beside the point. The repeated steps give the criticism a sense of one problem following another from the very beginning.
entries.usage_example: A draft plan has problems in its assumptions, costs and schedule. A reviewer quotes the saying to explain why changing one small detail will not address the whole. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: The verse pictures the date palm as marked with steps from its base. Repeating ପାହାଚ makes that succession audible; the source gloss turns it into an image of pervasive faults, while the question about virtues supplies the irony.

entries.title: Can persuasion make someone one’s own?
entries.odia:
ଖଣ୍ଡରେ ମୋହିଁଲେ କ୍ଷୀରରେ ଧୋଇଲେ
ଲିମ୍ବ କି ମଧୁର ହୋଇବ
ଯେତେ ପରକାରେ ବୁଝାଇ କହିଲେ
ପର କି ଆପଣା ହୋଇବ।
entries.literal_meaning: Even if treated with sugar and washed in milk, will neem become sweet? However many ways you explain and persuade, will an outsider become one of your own?
entries.meaning_odia: ଖଣ୍ଡ ଓ କ୍ଷୀରରେ ଲିମ୍ବର ତିକ୍ତତା ବଦଳିବ କି ବୋଲି ପଚାରି, ବକ୍ତା ପର ଲୋକକୁ କଥା କହି ବୁଝାଇ ଆପଣା କରିବା ସମ୍ଭବ କି ନାହିଁ ବୋଲି ସନ୍ଦେହ କରୁଛି। ଏହା ବକ୍ତାର ସନ୍ଦେହ; ପର ଲୋକଙ୍କ ସହ ଆତ୍ମୀୟତା ଗଢ଼ିପାରିବ ନାହିଁ ବୋଲି ସାଧାରଣ ସତ୍ୟ ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The speaker compares attempts to sweeten neem with attempts to turn an outsider into someone close through persuasion. Both rhetorical questions lean towards doubt. The verse voices distrust of a hoped-for change in allegiance or belonging; that distrust belongs to its speaker.
entries.usage_example: In a fictional dispute, someone disappointed by repeated failed attempts at reconciliation quotes the verse. It conveys their distrust at that moment. This illustration is newly composed.
entries.cultural_context: Sugar and milk are placed against neem’s bitter taste, then the verse moves from taste to the contrast between ପର and ଆପଣା. The repeated question ହୋଇବ links the two attempts at transformation. In the literal translation, “treated with sugar” keeps the first action broad because the exact physical sense of ମୋହିଁଲେ is unresolved.

witnesses.locator: Page13, four lines beginning ଖଣ୍ଡରେ ମୋହିଁଲେ.

entries.title: Ready to eat, unable to ululate
entries.odia:
ଖାଇଲା ବେଳକୁ ସାତ ପୁଅ ମା
ହୁଳହୁଳି ଦେଲା ବେଳକୁ ଜିଭରେ ଘା।
entries.literal_meaning: At eating time, a mother of seven sons; at ululation time, a sore on the tongue.
entries.meaning_odia: ଖାଇବା ବେଳେ ସାତ ପୁଅର ମା, ହୁଳହୁଳି ଦେବା ବେଳେ ଜିଭରେ ଘା—ଏହି ଦୁଇ ଅବସ୍ଥାକୁ ଯୋଡ଼ି କଥାଟି ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କରେ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ନିଜେ ସୁବିଧା ଭୋଗ କରିବାକୁ ଆଗ୍ରହ, କିନ୍ତୁ ନିଜ ଭାଗର ସହଯୋଗ ଦେବା ବେଳେ ଅସୁବିଧା ଦେଖାଇବା ପ୍ରତି ଇଙ୍ଗିତ ଅଛି।
entries.explanation: The two occasions expose a change in readiness: the first announces a mother of seven sons at mealtime, while the second produces a tongue too sore for an ululating cry. Our editorial reading hears a complaint about enjoying the benefits while finding an obstacle when participation is expected. The joke lies in the convenient contrast between the two moments.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: Someone eagerly joins a shared meal but repeatedly withdraws when the group asks for help preparing its next gathering. Another participant quotes the saying about willingness that changes with the occasion.
entries.cultural_context: The repeated ବେଳକୁ sets the occasions side by side. Eating and ululating both involve the mouth, making the tongue’s sudden prominence in the second line pointed. The literal mother-of-seven image lends the opening an expansive tone before the short complaint about a sore closes it.

entries.title: After eating, why should I go?
entries.odia:
ଖାଇ ସାରିଲେ ଗାଈ କି ଯିବି
ଖାଇ ସାରିଲି କାହିଁକି ଯିବି?
entries.literal_meaning: Once I have eaten, I will go to the cow. I have finished eating—why should I go?
entries.meaning_odia: ଖାଇବା ପୂର୍ବରୁ ଗାଈ ପାଖକୁ ଯିବାର କଥା ଦେଉଛି; ଖାଇସାରିଲା ପରେ କାହିଁକି ଯିବି ବୋଲି ଓଲଟା ପଚାରୁଛି। ନିଜ ସ୍ୱାର୍ଥ ପୂରଣ ହୋଇଗଲେ ଆଗର ପ୍ରତିଶ୍ରୁତିରୁ ଓହରିଯିବାକୁ ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଇଙ୍ଗିତ କରେ।
entries.explanation: Before the meal, eating is presented as the condition for going. After the meal, the same speaker questions any need to go at all. The inspected source gloss reads this as withdrawing once one’s own purpose has been served. The small change from “once I have eaten” to “I have eaten” exposes the broken promise.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: Someone promises to help carry supplies after receiving their meal. Once served, they refuse to help. A companion quotes the saying to recall the promise made before eating.
entries.cultural_context: The cow gives the promise a concrete destination. Repeating eating and going in both lines makes the reversal sharp: the meal first delays the undertaking and then becomes the point after which it is abandoned.

entries.title: Yesterday’s scraps, today’s rejected fritters
entries.odia:
ଖୁଣ୍ଟି ଖାଉଥିଲୁ ମଦରଙ୍ଗା ଶାଗ
ପିଠି ଖାଉଥିଲା ଖରା
କାଲି ଚାଟୁଥିଲୁ ଅଇଁଠା ପତର
ଆଜି ରୁଚୁ ନାହିଁ ବରା।
entries.literal_meaning: You used to pick and eat madaranga greens; your back took the sun. Yesterday you licked a used eating leaf; today fritters do not please your taste.
entries.meaning_odia: ଆଗେ ମଦରଙ୍ଗା ଶାଗ ଖୁଣ୍ଟି ଖାଇବା, ଖରାରେ ପିଠି ରହିବା ଓ ଅଇଁଠା ପତର ଚାଟିବାର କଥା ମନେ ପକାଇ ବକ୍ତା ଆଜି ବରା ନରୁଚିବାକୁ ଟାହି କରୁଛି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଅବସ୍ଥା ବଦଳିବା ସହ ରୁଚି ଓ ଆଚରଣ ବଦଳିଯିବା ପ୍ରତି ଏହି ଆକ୍ଷେପ; ଅଭାବରେ ଥିବା ଲୋକଙ୍କୁ ହେୟ କରିବା ଏହାର ସମ୍ପାଦକୀୟ ଅର୍ଥ ନୁହେଁ।
entries.explanation: The speaker sets remembered hardship against a newly fastidious appetite. Greens, sun on the back and scraps on an eating leaf build the first picture; rejected fritters provide the sharp reversal. Our editorial reading hears a taunt that the addressee has forgotten earlier circumstances. The contempt in that accusation belongs to the speaker.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a discussion of the verse, a reader notices how yesterday and today compress a change in circumstances. Another points out that the taunt reveals the speaker’s resentment as well as the addressee’s changed taste.
entries.cultural_context: The word for eating recurs in the image of the back taking the sun, linking hunger with exposure. The final contrast moves from licking remnants to finding fritters unappealing. Its force comes from the speaker’s pointed arrangement of those images.

entries.title: I provided, another gained authority
entries.odia:
ଖୋଇଲି ପେଇଲି ନ ହେଲି କିଛି
ଅଧିକାର କଲା ଗୁହାଳ ପୋଛି।
entries.literal_meaning: I fed and gave drink, yet became nothing; another gained authority by cleaning the cowshed.
entries.meaning_odia: ଖାଇବା ପିଇବା ଦେଇ ମଧ୍ୟ ନିଜେ କିଛି ହେଲି ନାହିଁ, ଅଥଚ ଗୁହାଳ ପୋଛି ଅନ୍ୟ ଜଣେ ଅଧିକାର ପାଇଲା—ଏହା ବକ୍ତାର ଅଭିଯୋଗ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ନିଜ ଅବଦାନର ସ୍ୱୀକୃତି ନମିଳି ଅନ୍ୟ ଜଣଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଭାବ ବଢ଼ିବାର କ୍ଷୋଭ ଶୁଣାଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: The speaker places two contributions side by side: providing food and drink, and cleaning a cowshed. The first, the speaker complains, brought no standing; the second brought someone else authority. Our editorial reading hears resentment at the difference between effort and recognition. The verse gives the speaker’s comparison, leaving the people and their arrangement unnamed.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a reading discussion, someone hears a complaint that providing resources did not bring influence while another person’s daily work did. A second reader asks whether the speaker’s resentment tells the whole story. The exchange explores the verse’s perspective.
entries.cultural_context: The first-person feeding verbs end in the self-effacing “became nothing.” The next line shifts to another person gaining authority, with cowshed cleaning as the concrete action. That change of grammatical person makes the unequal outcomes audible.

entries.title: Wherever you go, karma goes with you
entries.odia: ଗଙ୍ଗା ଯା ଗୟା ଯା କର୍ମ ଘେନି ବୁଲୁଥା।
entries.literal_meaning: Go to the Ganga, go to Gaya; keep wandering with your karma.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗଙ୍ଗାକୁ ଯାଅ କି ଗୟାକୁ ଯାଅ, ନିଜ କର୍ମ ସାଙ୍ଗରେ ରହିଥାଏ। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ସବୁ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରେ କର୍ମର ପ୍ରାଧାନ୍ୟ କହେ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ସ୍ଥାନ ବଦଳାଇଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ନିଜ କର୍ମ ଓ ତାହାର ପରିଣାମକୁ ପଛରେ ଛାଡ଼ି ଯାଇହୁଏ ନାହିଁ।
entries.explanation: The repeated invitation to go offers two sacred destinations, then adds what the traveller carries everywhere: karma. The inspected source gloss stresses its continuing importance. Our editorial reading hears a reminder that a change of place does not by itself separate a person from their deeds and consequences.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A reader discussing the verse says that changing one’s surroundings is not the same as addressing the consequences of earlier actions. The saying supplies the image of something carried along on every journey.
entries.cultural_context: Ganga and Gaya place the journey in a pilgrimage frame. The short repeated ଯା gives movement to the opening, while ଘେନି makes karma something that travels with the person. The verse’s force rests on that contrast between changing destinations and a continuing companion.

entries.title: The journey and its disappointing fruit
entries.odia: ଗଙ୍ଗା ଗଲି ଯେତିକି ଫଳ ପାଇଲି ସେତିକି।
entries.literal_meaning: As much as I went to the Ganga, that much fruit I received.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗଙ୍ଗାକୁ ଯିବା ଓ ସେଥିରୁ ମିଳିଥିବା ଫଳକୁ ବକ୍ତା ଯୋଡ଼ି କହୁଛି। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଏହାକୁ କୌଣସି ବିଷୟ ବା କାମରେ ଅତୃପ୍ତିର ପ୍ରକାଶ ବୋଲି କହେ। ତେଣୁ ଏଠାରେ ନିଜ ଉଦ୍ୟମର ଫଳକୁ ନେଇ ସନ୍ତୋଷ ନମିଳିବାର ସ୍ୱର ଶୁଣାଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: The sentence balances going to the Ganga against the fruit received. Although its surface wording pairs “as much” with “that much,” the inspected gloss identifies dissatisfaction with an undertaking. That gloss guides the reading toward an unimpressed reckoning of the outcome, rather than praise for a reward exactly proportional to effort.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: After completing an elaborate application process, someone finds the outcome disappointing and quotes the saying. The journey stands for the undertaking and its fruit for the result.
entries.cultural_context: The Ganga supplies the image of a journey associated with hoped-for benefit. The matched ଯେତିକି and ସେତିକି make the sentence sound like a compact reckoning. The inspected gloss gives that reckoning its dissatisfied tone.

entries.title: Poverty made a pretext for mockery
entries.odia: ଗରିବ ମାଇପ ସବୁରି ଶାଳୀ।
entries.literal_meaning: A poor man’s wife is everyone’s sister-in-law (wife’s sister).
entries.meaning_odia: ଗରିବ ଲୋକର ସ୍ତ୍ରୀକୁ ସମସ୍ତେ ନିଜ ଶାଳୀ ବୋଲି ଧରିନେବାର ରୂପକ ଏଠାରେ ଅଛି। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଅନୁସାରେ ଦାରିଦ୍ର୍ୟର ସୁଯୋଗ ନେଇ ଲୋକେ ଥଟ୍ଟା ପରିହାସ କରନ୍ତି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଏହା ଅସମ୍ମାନ ଓ ଅନଧିକାର ଘନିଷ୍ଠତାର ଛବି; ଦାରିଦ୍ର୍ୟ କାହାର ସମ୍ମାନ କମାଏ ନାହିଁ।
entries.explanation: The saying makes an impossible family claim: everyone treats the poor man’s wife as their own sister-in-law. The inspected gloss explains this as taking advantage of poverty to mock people. Our reading focuses on the disrespect in that claimed familiarity, rather than treating poverty as a reason anyone deserves it.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A discussion turns to people who ridicule a neighbour because the household has little money. Someone cites the proverb as a sharp image of that disrespect and challenges the mockery.
entries.cultural_context: The kinship word ଶାଳୀ supplies a claim of personal familiarity, while ସବୁରି expands that claim to everyone. The source gloss links this intrusion to poverty. The woman in the image carries the insult directed at a household’s vulnerable position.

entries.title: Refusing when called upon
entries.odia:
ଗାଆଣକୁ ଗାଆ କହିଲେ ଗାଏ ନାହିଁ
ଡାହାଣୀକୁ ଖାଆ କହିଲେ ଖାଏ ନାହିଁ
entries.literal_meaning: Tell the singer to sing, and the singer does not sing; tell the witch to eat, and she does not eat.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗାଇବାକୁ କହିଲେ ଗାଆଣ ଗାଏ ନାହିଁ, ଖାଇବାକୁ କହିଲେ କଥାର ଡାହାଣୀ ଖାଏ ନାହିଁ। ଉତ୍ସ ଏହି ଅମଙ୍ଗକୁ ନିଜ ଗୁମର ପଦାରେ ପଡ଼ିଯିବାର ଭୟ ସହ ଯୋଡ଼େ। କିଛି ଲୁଚାଇ ରଖିବା ପାଇଁ ସମ୍ମୁଖରେ କାମଟି କରିବାକୁ ନଚାହିଁବାର ଛବି ଏଠାରେ ଅଛି।
entries.explanation: Each figure refuses the very action named in the request. The inspected gloss attributes that reluctance to fear of exposing a secret. The parallel turns an apparently simple invitation into a moment of guardedness; it leaves the secret itself unspecified.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a literary discussion, readers ask why both figures refuse. One points to the source gloss about concealment, while another observes that the verse never tells us what the singer is hiding.
entries.cultural_context: The repeated pattern of command and refusal binds the lines together, and the close sounds of ଗାଆ and ଖାଆ sharpen the pairing. The witch belongs to the verse’s imagined comparison. Its discussion of concealment can be read without applying that label to a real person.

entries.title: Struck or striking, I am done for
entries.odia:
ଗାଈ ମାଇଲେ ମଲି
ଗାଈକି ମାଇଲେ ମଲି।
entries.literal_meaning: If the cow strikes me, I am done for; if I strike the cow, I am done for.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗାଈ ମୋତେ ମାରିଲେ ବିପଦ, ମୁଁ ଗାଈକୁ ମାରିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ବିପଦ—ଦୁଇ ପଟୁ ଅଡ଼ୁଆର ଛବି। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଏହାକୁ ଦୋସନ୍ଧିରେ ପଡ଼ି କଣ କରିବା ଉଚିତ ନିର୍ଣ୍ଣୟ କରି ନପାରିବା ସହ ଯୋଡ଼େ।
entries.explanation: The cow first does the striking, then receives it, but the speaker’s predicament remains unchanged. The inspected gloss identifies a dilemma in which deciding what to do becomes difficult. The repeated “I am done for” makes both alternatives feel closed off.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A coordinator faces two incompatible requests; accepting either will disappoint the other group. The saying expresses feeling trapped between the alternatives.
entries.cultural_context: Adding କି changes the cow from the doer of the action to its object. That tiny grammatical shift reverses who strikes whom, while ମଲି remains the same at each line’s end. The force of the saying lies in the speaker being in trouble under both arrangements.

entries.title: The poor ox belongs to no one
entries.odia:
ଗାଈ ସହଦେବଙ୍କର
ଷଣ୍ଢ ମହାଦେବଙ୍କର
ବଳଦ ବାପୁଡା କହାରି ନୁହେଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: The cow belongs to Sahadeva; the bull belongs to Mahadeva; the poor ox belongs to no one.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗାଈ ପାଇଁ ସହଦେବଙ୍କ ନାମ, ଷଣ୍ଢ ପାଇଁ ମହାଦେବଙ୍କ ନାମ ଅଛି; ବଳଦ ବାପୁଡାର କେହି ନାହିଁ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଅନ୍ୟମାନଙ୍କର ଆପଣା ଲୋକ ବା ସାହାରା ଥିବା ବେଳେ ଜଣେ ଏକା ଓ ଅବହେଳିତ ରହିଯିବାର କ୍ଷୋଭ ଓ କରୁଣା ଏଠାରେ ଶୁଣାଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: The first two lines give the cow and bull a named affiliation. The third breaks the pattern: the ox has nobody. Our editorial reading hears sympathy for someone left without support while others have a person to whom they belong. The affectionate pity in “poor ox” gives the ending its emotional weight.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a group where most people can turn to a supporter, one member feels overlooked. A reader uses the saying’s final line to describe that feeling of having nobody in their corner.
entries.cultural_context: The repeated possessive endings after Sahadeva and Mahadeva establish an expectation of belonging. The ox’s line replaces a name with “no one.” Cow, bull and ox stay distinct in the translation so that the three-part comparison remains visible.

entries.title: Used up a little at a time
entries.odia:
ଗୁଡ ଚାଖୁ ଚାଖୁ ଯାଏ
ତେଲ ମାଖୁ ମାଖୁ ଯାଏ।
entries.literal_meaning: Jaggery goes as you keep tasting it; oil goes as you keep applying it.
entries.meaning_odia: ବାରମ୍ବାର ଅଳ୍ପ ଅଳ୍ପ ଚାଖିଲେ ଗୁଡ ସରେ, ଅଳ୍ପ ଅଳ୍ପ ମାଖିଲେ ତେଲ ସରେ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଛୋଟ ଛୋଟ ବ୍ୟବହାରର ମୋଟ ପରିମାଣକୁ ଧ୍ୟାନ ଦେବାର କଥା ଏଠାରେ ଅଛି—ଥରକୁ ଅଳ୍ପ ଲାଗିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ବାରମ୍ବାର ହେଲେ ଭଣ୍ଡାର କମିଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: Each taste or application may seem small, but repetition draws down the supply. Our editorial reading connects the two everyday actions as an image of gradual depletion. The verse makes the accumulating effect noticeable through its repeated verbs.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: Small withdrawals from a shared supply seem negligible until the container is nearly empty. Someone quotes the saying to explain how repeated little uses add up.
entries.cultural_context: ଚାଖୁ ଚାଖୁ and ମାଖୁ ମାଖୁ echo each other in sound and rhythm. One line tastes, the other applies, but both end with ଯାଏ: the substance is going. The paired structure turns repetition itself into the explanation.

entries.title: Can fine qualities become a drink?
entries.odia:
ଗୁଣ ସୁନ୍ଦର ବୋଲି ଗୋଳି ପିଇବ କି
ରୂପ ସୁନ୍ଦର ବୋଲି ପାରି ଶୋଇବ କି?
entries.literal_meaning: Because its qualities are fine, will you mix it up and drink it? Because its appearance is beautiful, will you spread it out and sleep on it?
entries.meaning_odia: ଗୁଣ ଭଲ ବୋଲି କଣ ତାକୁ ଗୋଳି ପିଇହେବ, ରୂପ ସୁନ୍ଦର ବୋଲି କଣ ତାକୁ ବିଛାଇ ଶୋଇହେବ—ଏହି ଦୁଇ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କଥାଟିର ଆଧାର। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଗୁଣ ବା ରୂପର ପ୍ରଶଂସା ମାତ୍ରରେ ସବୁ ବ୍ୟବହାରିକ ଆବଶ୍ୟକତା ପୂରଣ ହୁଏ ନାହିଁ; କେଉଁ କାମରେ କଣ ଲାଗିବ, ତାହା ମଧ୍ୟ ବିଚାର କରିବାକୁ ହୁଏ।
entries.explanation: The two questions turn praise into deliberately awkward practical tests: can admired qualities be mixed into a drink, or beauty spread out to sleep on? Our editorial reading distinguishes admiration from usefulness for a particular need. The verse leaves its target unnamed, so the comparison can remain broad.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A group admires an object’s finish but finds it unsuitable for the job they need done. A reader recalls the verse’s questions to distinguish what is attractive from what serves the purpose.
entries.cultural_context: The repeated ସୁନ୍ଦର ବୋଲି introduces a reason that each question then tests. Drinking and sleeping are concrete actions placed against abstract qualities and appearance. Their mismatch gives the questions their sceptical force.

entries.title: Caught up in the herd’s excitement
entries.odia: ଗୋଠ ମାତିଲେ ଖଣ୍ଡିଆ ମାତେ।
entries.literal_meaning: When the herd gets excited, even its weak animal gets excited.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗୋଠ ମାତିଲେ ସେଥିରେ ଥିବା ଦୁର୍ବଳ ପଶୁଟି ମଧ୍ୟ ମାତିଉଠେ। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଅନୁସାରେ ଦଳର ଅନ୍ୟମାନଙ୍କ ଉତ୍ସାହରେ ନିଜେ କମ୍ ସମର୍ଥ ଥିବା ଜଣେ ମଧ୍ୟ ସାମିଲ ହୋଇଯାଏ। ଦଳର ଆବେଗ ଜଣକଠାରୁ ଅନ୍ୟଜଣଙ୍କୁ ବ୍ୟାପିବାର ଛବି ଏଠାରେ ଅଛି।
entries.explanation: The herd’s excitement carries even its weaker member along. The inspected gloss applies this to members of a group who become animated with the others despite having less strength or ability on their own. The focus is the spread of collective excitement.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A usually hesitant participant joins in when a whole group grows enthusiastic about a performance. A reader recalls the herd image to describe being swept up in a shared mood.
entries.cultural_context: The same verb frames the herd and its singled-out member, showing the group’s mood repeated in the individual. The public counterpart adds ହଡ଼ା, an old bullock, beside ଖଣ୍ଡିଆ. That supports the contrast with a less vigorous animal without requiring an invented injury.

entries.title: Pursue without catching, raise without striking
entries.odia:
ଗୋଡାଉଥିବୁ ଧରିବୁ ନାଇଁ
ଉଞ୍ଚାଉଥିବୁ ମାରିବୁ ନାଇଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: Keep chasing, but do not catch; keep raising, but do not strike.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗୋଡ଼ାଇବ, କିନ୍ତୁ ଧରିବ ନାହିଁ; ଉଞ୍ଚାଇବ, କିନ୍ତୁ ମାରିବ ନାହିଁ। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟାରେ ଏହା ପ୍ରକୃତ ଦଣ୍ଡ ନଦେଇ ଭୟ ଦେଖାଇ କାମ ହାସଲ କରିବାର କଥା। ଉଭୟ ଧାଡ଼ିରେ ଆରମ୍ଭ କରାଯାଇଥିବା କ୍ରିୟାର ଶେଷ ପଦକ୍ଷେପକୁ ଅଟକାଇ ରଖାଯାଏ।
entries.explanation: Both lines begin an action and forbid its completion. The inspected gloss presents this as using the display of a threat instead of carrying out punishment. The saying’s tension lies between visible pursuit or preparation and the deliberately withheld act.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a discussion of a story, a character repeatedly threatens action but stops before carrying it out. A reader quotes the saying to describe that pattern and asks what effect the threats have on others.
entries.cultural_context: The parallel commands give pursuit and a raised gesture the same stopping point. Each line ends in refusal: no catching, no striking. The source treats that gap between threat and action as a method of control; the verse itself names neither a weapon nor a target.

entries.title: Crossing with another’s support
entries.odia: ଗୋରୁ ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ ଧରି ବୈତରଣୀ ପାରି।
entries.literal_meaning: Crossing the Vaitarani while holding a cow’s tail.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗୋରୁର ଲାଙ୍ଗୁଡ ଧରି ବୈତରଣୀ ପାର ହେବାର ଛବି। ଉତ୍ସର ବ୍ୟାଖ୍ୟା ଅନୁସାରେ ନିଜେ ପାର ହେବାକୁ ଅସମର୍ଥ ଥିବା ବେଳେ ଅନ୍ୟର ସାହାରା ଧରି ଉଦ୍ଧାର ପାଇବାକୁ ଏହା ତୁଳନା କରେ।
entries.explanation: The crossing is accomplished through something the traveller can hold onto. The inspected gloss uses the image for getting through a difficulty with another’s support when one cannot manage alone. Its emphasis is reliance on help.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: An inexperienced organiser completes a demanding task with sustained guidance from a colleague. Looking back, they use the saying to acknowledge the support that carried them through.
entries.cultural_context: The named river gives the obstacle a concrete form, and the held tail gives support a physical shape. The source explains the crossing as a simile of reliance; the image remains proverbial rather than a claim that such a crossing or religious deliverance has occurred.

entries.title: All yours, but touch nothing
entries.odia:
ଘର ଦୁଆର ସବୁ ତୋର
କାହିଁରେ ନଦେବୁ ହାତ।
entries.literal_meaning: The house and doorway are all yours; do not lay a hand on anything.
entries.meaning_odia: ଘର ଦୁଆର ସବୁ ତୋର ବୋଲି କହି, ପୁଣି କୌଣସି ଜିନିଷରେ ହାତ ଦେବାକୁ ମନା କରାଯାଉଛି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଏହି ବିରୋଧ କଥାରେ ଅଧିକାର ବା ଆଦର ଦେଖାଇ ବାସ୍ତବରେ ବ୍ୟବହାରର ସୁଯୋଗ ନଦେବାକୁ ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ କରେ।
entries.explanation: The first line appears to give everything; the second prevents even a touch. Our editorial reading hears hollow generosity or authority granted only in words. The contradiction makes the promise collapse as soon as the listener tries to imagine using it.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: Someone is told a shared room is theirs to use, but every proposed use is then forbidden. They quote the saying to describe permission that exists only in words.
entries.cultural_context: ସବୁ makes the offer sweeping, and କାହିଁରେ makes the restriction equally sweeping. The ordinary act of putting out a hand tests the claim of belonging: the person addressed may be told everything is theirs but cannot act on that assurance.

entries.title: Let the house burn, so the mice get some of it
entries.odia:
ଘର ପୋଡିଯାଉ ପଛେ
ମୂଷା ପାଆନ୍ତି କେଞ୍ଚେ।
entries.literal_meaning: Let the house burn, so long as the mice get a little of it.
entries.meaning_odia: ଘର ପୋଡ଼ିଯାଉ ପଛେ ମୂଷାମାନେ ଟିକିଏ ପାଆନ୍ତୁ—କଥାଟିରେ ଏପରି ଜିଦ୍ ଶୁଣାଯାଏ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଅନ୍ୟକୁ କିଛି କଷ୍ଟ ଦେବାର ସନ୍ତୋଷ ପାଇଁ ବହୁତ ବଡ଼ କ୍ଷତିକୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ମାନିନେବାର ବ୍ୟଙ୍ଗ ଅଛି। ଘରର ବଡ଼ କ୍ଷତି ଓ ମୂଷାଙ୍କର ଅଳ୍ପ ପ୍ରାପ୍ତି ମଧ୍ୟରେ ତଫାତ ଏହାକୁ ତୀକ୍ଷ୍ଣ କରେ।
entries.explanation: The house can be lost, provided the mice receive even a little of what happens. Our editorial reading hears spite overriding proportion: a large loss becomes acceptable for the satisfaction of hurting a target. A located literary use places a close variant in a retaliatory context.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: In a dispute, someone is willing to ruin a shared project merely to deny a rival a small advantage. Another participant quotes the saying to expose the disproportionate cost of that spite.
entries.cultural_context: The concessive ପଛେ pushes the burning house aside as an acceptable cost. କେଞ୍ଚେ then reduces the desired effect on the mice to a little. That imbalance between a whole house and a small retaliatory satisfaction drives the irony.

entries.title: House fire and horseback prosperity
entries.odia:
ଘର ପୋଡିରୁ ବିପତ୍ତି ନାଇଁ
ଘୋଡ଼ା ଚଢ଼ାରୁ ସମ୍ପତ୍ତି ନାଇଁ।
entries.literal_meaning: No calamity is greater than a house fire; no prosperity is greater than riding a horse.
entries.meaning_odia: ଘର ପୋଡ଼ିଠାରୁ ବଡ଼ ବିପତ୍ତି ନାହିଁ, ଘୋଡ଼ା ଚଢ଼ାଠାରୁ ବଡ଼ ସମ୍ପତ୍ତି ନାହିଁ—ଏପରି ଅତିଶୟ ତୁଳନା କଥାଟି କରେ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଗୋଟିଏ ଛବି ବଡ଼ କ୍ଷତିର, ଅନ୍ୟଟି ସମୃଦ୍ଧିର। ଦୁଇ ବିପରୀତ ଅବସ୍ଥାକୁ ମନରେ ଗାଢ଼ କରିବା ଏହାର ଢଙ୍ଗ।
entries.explanation: The saying places a burning home and a mounted rider at opposite ends of fortune. Its comparative wording presents each as unsurpassed: one in calamity, the other in prosperity. Our editorial reading treats those extremes as proverbial emphasis rather than a literal ranking of every possible loss or kind of wealth.
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A discussion of the verse contrasts losing the security of home with a conspicuous image of prosperity. Readers notice how the two lines compress those extremes into memorable pictures.
entries.cultural_context: ବିପତ୍ତି and ସମ୍ପତ୍ତି rhyme while naming opposite conditions. The matching negative endings intensify each comparison: nothing exceeds this. Horse riding serves as the saying’s chosen image of prosperity, paired with the destruction of a home.
